title: Coda — Sense of Place
paragraphs: The book ends in Basso's own voice, generalising carefully from Cibecue. Places, he argues, have a marked capacity for triggering acts of self-reflection — thoughts about who one presently is, memories of who one used to be, musings on who one might become. And such thoughts do not stay put: they lead to other places, other people, other times, whole networks of association that ramify within the expanding spheres of awareness they themselves create. Sensing places is thoroughly reciprocal and incorrigibly dynamic. When places are actively sensed, the physical landscape becomes wedded to the landscape of the mind, and where that may lead is anybody's guess.

He insists that relationships to places are not only verbal. They find expression through myth, prayer, music, dance, art, architecture, and in many communities through recurrent religious and political ritual — enacted daily, monthly, seasonally, annually, until places and their meanings are woven into the fabric of social life. That is what makes the omission from anthropology so odd. Where places are involved, modes of dwelling are never far behind, and in this dimly lit region of the anthropological world — call it, he offers, the ethnography of lived topographies — much remains to be learned.

The theory he leans on is compact. From Heidegger he takes dwelling: the multiple lived relationships people maintain with places, by virtue of which alone space acquires meaning, since spaces receive their essential being from particular localities and not from space itself. From Husserl he takes the question of how people discover that the world matters. From Camus he takes the correction that keeps the whole idea from floating off: sense of place is not just something people know and feel, it is something people do. And from Lawrence Durrell he takes the reminder that a sense of place, like every other sense we have invented, is inseparable from the ideas that inform it — everywhere parochial and everywhere specific.

Which returns him to the ethnographer's job. Naturally occurring depictions of places are to be treated as actualizations of the knowledge that informs them — native constructions wrought with native materials, displaying a native cast of mind — and it is that cast of mind the ethnographer must work to grasp and set down. He describes the ambition as heaven in a few grains of carefully inspected sand: instructive statements about places and their role in human affairs, reached through the close contextualization of a handful of telling events. Everything, or almost everything, hinges on the particulars, and because it does, ethnography is essential.

He allows himself two closing permissions. One is Isaiah Berlin's: better to write about what you believe you know something of than to anguish over the difficulty of knowing anything at all. The other is his own — that doing ethnography can be a great deal of fun, that disguising the fact on paper is less than honest and probably less than effective, and that in crafting prose as in fieldwork it is always permissible, and sometimes highly informative, to smile and even to laugh. The last word, though, belongs to the argument the whole book has been making: in modern landscapes everywhere people persist in asking what happened here, and what they make of their places is inseparable from what they make of themselves. We are, in a sense, the place-worlds we imagine.
